children: The Securities and Exchange Commission has charged a California registered investment advisor firm and its owner with an alleged cherry-picking scheme that regulators say allocated losing trades to clients while the advisor pocketed the proceeds from profitable transactions.

The charges against Darren Caris and Caris Investment Partners, based in the San Diego suburb of Encinitas, allege that Caris traded clients' funds through a block-trading account, enabling him to allocate trades to the various accounts over which he had discretion.

"Caris submitted these allocations to a brokerage firm well after he placed the trades and observed share-price movement, giving him the opportunity to 'cherry-pick' — that is, disproportionately allocate winning trades to his personal account and disproportionately allocate losing trades to 16 client accounts," the SEC says in its complaint.

The SEC alleges that from December 2023 through April 2024, Caris allocated more than $158,000 in profitable trades to his personal account, while "client accounts suffered approximately $143,754 in first-day losses because of Caris' fraud." A statistical analysis found a less than one-in-a-million chance that those trading allocations could have resulted from random chance, "as opposed to knowing and intentional conduct," according to the SEC.

Caris' lawyer, Robert Brownlie, says his client denies the allegations and "did not engage in 'cherry picking.'" Brownlie says that commission staffers explained during the investigation that their allegations were based on a statistical analysis of just three client accounts over a period of four months.

"That analysis did not show that Mr. Caris allocated trades after the outcomes were known but only that it was statistically improbable that the allocation of trades was random," Brownlie says. "Indeed, the allocation was not random."

Brownlie says that Caris distinguished his own trades from those of his clients and ensured that all trades were properly allocated. He says that the three clients involved in the statistical analysis that the SEC presented during the investigation made more than $375,000 during the relevant period. "Mr. Caris intends to defend and vindicate himself against the Commission's allegations," he says.

The case is the latest reminder that cherry-picking remains a top concern for regulators and law-enforcement authorities. Earlier this week, the SEC asked a court to approve a final judgment against Kenneth Leech, a prominent bond fund manager and the former co-chief investment officer at Western Asset Management Company, a unit of Franklin Templeton, for his role in an alleged cherry-picking scheme that saw hundreds of millions of dollars allocated to preferred or disfavored client accounts based on the performance of the trades. A representative of Franklin Templeton didn't immediately respond to a request for comment on the Western Asset settlement.

The proposed settlement would require Leech to pay a $3 million penalty and accept a bar from the industry. In June, the SEC announced a settlement with Western Asset, which agreed to pay $100 million to address the cherry-picking allegations without admitting or denying wrongdoing.

In a criminal matter, Leech has pleaded guilty to obstruction of justice for providing false and misleading testimony in the SEC's investigation. He is awaiting sentencing. Lawyers for Leech declined to comment on the case.

Another recent cherry-picking case involved William Carlton, a former Cetera advisor whom the SEC accused of claiming $5.3 million in profitable trades for himself while saddling his clients with losing trades. In September, Carlton pleaded guilty to securities fraud in a criminal case. His sentencing is scheduled for January 27. Carlton's lawyer didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

In the case of Caris and his RIA, the scale of the alleged fraud is far smaller than Leech or Carlton, but the case aligns with the direction the SEC says it is taking under Chairman Paul Atkins, who has said the commission should focus more on rooting out investor fraud than pursuing settlements with financial services firms for technical rule violations that amount to no direct investor harm.
This isn't Caris' first run-in with securities regulators.

Last October, Caris settled charges with California authorities who accused him of defrauding his own children, saying that he improperly siphoned money out of their accounts for his personal use. California had initially sought to bar Caris from the industry, but the parties later reached a settlement fining the advisor $10,000 and ordering him to pay $167,000 in disgorgement — $119,000 to one of his children and $48,000 to the other. Caris reached that settlement without admitting or denying wrongdoing.
